node.dia-daq-read.help: Reads samples from a data acquisition task on NI hardware, through NI's gRPC Device Server. The host the hardware is attached to needs NI's DAQmx driver and the NI gRPC Device Server, started with a configuration that turns on TLS, and with an address other than localhost if Flow runs on another machine. Never leave the server's unsecured port open on a plant network: set Security to on, or to mutual to also check this node's own certificate. Finite mode takes one acquisition of the samples you set on every call. Continuous mode starts the task on the first call and reads the next block of samples on each call after it. y is the samples of one channel as an array, or an array of arrays, one per channel in order. dt is the seconds between samples. A refusal from the server or the driver is an error on the error wire with the driver's own code and text. The task is cleared on the server when the run ends. node.dia-filter.help: A Butterworth filter: flat in the band it passes, with no ripple, and 3 dB down at the cutoff. Lowpass keeps what is slower than the cutoff, highpass keeps what is faster, bandpass keeps what is between the two edges, and bandstop removes it. A higher order cuts off more sharply and rings a little longer after a step. The cutoff must be above zero and below half the sample rate. Give it an array, or one number at a time, and it remembers where it was between calls in a run, so a signal cut into pieces is filtered as one. The rate input wins over the Samples per second property. It starts from rest, so the first samples of an array carry a start-up settle; it delays the signal by an amount that depends on frequency, so it is wrong to use where the timing between two signals has to line up exactly; and it is not a linear-phase or zero-phase filter.

A file that already exists is appended to, so runs follow each other in one file, and a file cut short by a power loss is repaired to its last complete row before the new rows go on. node.exec.compat: The three outputs, both buffered and streaming modes, the timeout and the appended message property all behave as Node-RED's do. Two things do not, and neither is negotiable. There is no shell: the command line is split on quoting rules only, and an unquoted shell metacharacter is refused rather than run, so one allowed command cannot become an arbitrary one. And the node is disabled until an operator names the commands a flow may run. Node-RED's exec node runs anything, and Node-RED starts with no authentication by default; a vendor shipping that default became CVE-2025-41656 (Pilz IndustrialPI 4, VDE-2025-045), unauthenticated command execution on the device. Output is capped per stream; a command that exceeds it is killed and reported rather than being allowed to fill the heap. A command that forks children of its own may leave them behind when it is killed.

node.function.compat: Runs on goja, a JavaScript interpreter written in Go, rather than Node's vm module. The language is ES2023; the Node standard library is not present. require() and npm modules do not work and cannot be made to without embedding Node. There is always a CPU time limit, which Node-RED leaves optional and off, and it applies to every timer callback too. setTimeout, setInterval and their clear functions work, on the node's clock, and every one is cleared when the flow stops or is redeployed. Buffer is there (alloc, from, concat, the read and write methods for integers and floats in both byte orders, slice, toString and toJSON). A byte slice in a message arrives as a byte array, so wrap it with Buffer.from.

node.http in.compat: Serves a path, with Express-style :params and a trailing *, and builds the same msg.req / msg.res / msg.payload shape Node-RED does, including JSON, form-encoded and raw bodies. Three deliberate differences. A request that no HTTP Response node answers is closed with 504 after a timeout instead of being held open forever, because Node-RED's version leaks a connection per request until the process runs out of sockets and stops answering with nothing in the log. Two nodes claiming the same method and path is refused at deploy time rather than one of them silently never firing. And a path that would shadow the editor or the admin API is refused for the same reason. Uploads parse the way multer does in Node-RED: text fields into msg.payload, files into msg.req.files, a broken upload answered with 500. One bound multer lacks: an array index over 10,000 in a field name, a[99999999], is refused instead of building a sparse array that long. msg.req.cookies is cookie-parser's, j: values included.

node.http request.compat: Method, URL, headers, basic authentication, redirects and the three return types, with msg.url, msg.method and msg.headers overriding the node. The response body is size-capped and the call is bounded by a timeout, neither of which Node-RED does. TLS comes from a tls-config, or without one msg.rejectUnauthorized = false skips the certificate check for that one message, as in Node-RED. msg.cookies and a cookie header go out through a cookie jar, cookies a redirect sets follow the redirect, and msg.responseCookies and msg.redirectList come back, all as in Node-RED. There is no egress allowlist: this node can reach anything the pod can, exactly as Node-RED's can, and the place to bound that is a NetworkPolicy rather than an edit dialog nobody outside the cluster can trust. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds the connections to one network interface.

node.mcp client.help:
Calls a tool on an MCP server when a message arrives, and sends the message on with the tool's answer in msg.payload. An answer that is structured is sent as an object; text is sent as text, and several pieces of text are joined with a newline. msg.mcp holds the server, the tool, and the answer's content exactly as the server sent it.

A tool that reports an error raises one, with the server's words, so a Catch node sees what the model would have seen. A call is never sent twice: if the connection fails halfway, the error says so and the next message connects again.
